interviewQuestions.question: Your test suite went from 3 minutes to 40 minutes over the last year as the codebase grew. How would you approach fixing that?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
First I'd establish where the time actually goes, because "40 minutes" hides very different problems depending on the shape — a few very slow tests, or thousands of individually-fine tests running serially. I'd pull per-test timing from CI history rather than guessing.

The direct fix is parallelizing and sharding: split the suite across multiple CI workers running concurrently, and shard by **historical runtime**, not test count or file count — a naive even split by file can put a few slow integration tests in one shard and leave it as the bottleneck while nine other shards finish early. Within a single worker, run independent tests concurrently on multiple cores too, which surfaces any shared-state bugs immediately since parallel execution breaks tests that secretly depended on running in a specific order.

Second, I'd stage the pipeline so the fastest, highest-signal checks run first and can short-circuit the rest: lint and unit tests in under 2 minutes, failing fast before spending any time on slower integration or e2e suites that would've caught the same regression eventually anyway.

The reason I'd prioritize this at all: suite runtime isn't just a CI cost line item, it changes developer behavior — under 2 minutes people wait and fix immediately; past 30 they push, context-switch, and come back to a red build having lost the context that would've made the fix trivial.

**Testing:** whether you treat suite speed as an engineering-behavior problem, not just an infrastructure cost.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Debugging

interviewQuestions.question: How do you decide whether to quarantine a flaky test, delete it, or block merges until it's fixed?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I match the option to the cause and the moment, not to a blanket policy. If the flake is in code someone is actively working on right now, I'd block on it — the context is fresh, the fix is cheap today and gets more expensive the longer it waits. If it's a long-standing flaky test whose underlying cause isn't urgent and isn't blocking anyone specific, I'd quarantine it — move it out of the merge-blocking path but keep it running and visible, with an owner and a deadline attached, not just silence. If investigation shows the test no longer verifies anything meaningful — testing a feature that's since been removed, or fully redundant with a better test elsewhere — I'd delete it outright rather than spend effort stabilizing something not worth keeping.

The failure mode I actively guard against is quarantine becoming a one-way door. Without an owner and expiry, quarantined tests accumulate for months because nothing forces anyone back to them — I've seen quarantine lists balloon into a second, silently-disabled suite that nobody remembers the reasoning behind. So whatever quarantine mechanism I set up comes with a dashboard showing age, an escalation past two weeks, and a real agreement that an unfixed quarantined test eventually gets deleted rather than living forever.

**Testing:** whether you can reason about the trade-off situationally instead of reaching for one default response to every flaky test.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: How does testing strategy change once you're operating dozens of microservices instead of one monolith?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The core problem is that broad integration testing — spin up every real service, run the full flow — stops scaling. With 30 services, verifying every consumer-provider pair live is roughly an O(services²) problem, and it's slow and flaky by nature since you're depending on that many real components being simultaneously healthy.

Contract testing is the answer at this scale: each consumer publishes its expectations (request/response shapes) to a shared broker, and each provider's own CI replays those contracts against its real implementation independently. That turns the quadratic problem into roughly a linear one — no consumer needs a live provider running, and no provider needs to spin up thirty live consumers to check compatibility. The broker becomes genuinely useful infrastructure: before a provider deploys a breaking change, it can check against every recorded consumer contract centrally and know exactly who it would break.

Test data management also changes shape — with many teams sharing infrastructure, fixture collisions become common, so synthetic data generation and per-test builders (rather than shared fixture files) matter more than they did with one team owning one database.

The throughline: at this scale, testing strategy is a systems-design problem in its own right — broker uptime, contract versioning, data isolation — not just "write more integration tests."

**Testing:** whether you can reason about testing as an organizational and infrastructural concern once service count multiplies, not just a per-service practice.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Systems at scale

interviewQuestions.question: Who should own test suite health at a large company — is it every engineer's job, or does it need a dedicated owner?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
In my experience "everyone's job" for test infrastructure specifically tends to mean nobody's job in practice — suite runtime creeps up, the quarantine list grows, and no single person feels responsible for reversing either trend because it's diffused across every team that contributes a test.

Individual test quality — is this one test well-written, does it assert on behavior, is it isolated — genuinely is every engineer's responsibility, the same way code quality broadly is. But suite-level properties — total runtime, sharding balance, quarantine policy and its expiry, the contract broker's uptime — behave like shared infrastructure, and shared infrastructure needs an explicit owner or it degrades the way any unowned commons does. I've seen teams get real traction by assigning a rotating or dedicated "test infra" owner (sometimes part of a platform team) whose job is specifically the suite's aggregate health metrics, distinct from any one team's feature tests.

The split I'd advocate for: engineers own the quality of the tests they write; a named owner or team owns the suite's collective behavior — speed, flake rate, quarantine hygiene — with visible dashboards so it's a tracked metric, not a vague aspiration everyone assumes someone else is handling.

**Testing:** whether you can distinguish individual practice from organizational ownership, and whether you'd actually name a concrete owner rather than deferring to "the team."
